items.title: Mike Wofford interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 13, 1998

ctx.x: could sit in a symphony orchestra, who could do all kinds of stuff. So there was nothing demeaning or ridiculous about being there, I mean you were lucky to be there. But a lot of times the product you were going for was maybe — this, we’re not talking here Pierre Boulez, but on the other hand, in many cases it was wonderful music, great writers who took it very seriously, even if it was just fairly innocuous film, took the writing very seriously. I worked for Dave Grusin a lot. Dave Grusin wrote beautiful stuff…
You want me to pause for a second? Yes, tell him I’ll call him a little bit later. Ray Conniff is coming tomorrow.

Oh. You let me know your time frame too, it’s two o’clock. So anyway, yeah, you know studio work was just something that happened. And about that same time jazz went into another one of its declines, you know the late ‘60s, early ‘70s was a very difficult time for jazz. I mean there have been all these valleys over there, and that was one of them. And at the time it just seemed like again it was partly survival. There’s no point in starving. I mean you just do what you have to do. And if there’d been more…
